#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when you need a one-off patch*
This scenario shows the direct form of the private-repository pattern: instead of importing a vendor BOM, the build requests the patched version of one dependency explicitly. It is simpler than the BOM route and suits a single patched artifact; it becomes verbose when many need overriding.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Gradle 8.14**.
Re-verified on Gradle 9.3 (October 2026): Gradle 9 raised the runtime floor to JDK 17 and changed defaults such as the configuration cache, not the resolution rules shown here.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    subgraph Public Repos
        SpringBoot["spring-boot-starter:2.5.14 (EOL)"]
    end
    subgraph Private Repo
        PatchedStarter["spring-boot-starter:2.5.14.ACME"]
    end
    Root[Project Root] -- declares --> PatchedStarter
```

The build adds the private repository and declares the patched version directly:

```{.groovy include="build.gradle" snippet="repo-and-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
Declaring `2.5.14.ACME` pins it: a direct declaration is the strongest signal there is.

#### ! Actual
`2.5.14.ACME` resolves, because nothing else in this graph asks for `spring-boot-starter` at all. A direct declaration is an ordinary `require`; had a transitive requested `2.6.0`, highest-wins would have selected that instead ([GS4](../scenario-4-override/guide.qmd)). The patch won by being unopposed, not by rank.

#### ! Why
Gradle looks for the requested version in the declared repositories in order; the private repository is the only one that has `2.5.14.ACME`, so it is found there. Selection, though, is still conflict resolution: every request for the module is pooled and the highest wins. To make a patched version unconditional, declare it with `version { strictly '2.5.14.ACME' }`, or put the pin in an enforced platform ([GS16](../scenario-16-private-bom/guide.qmd)).

#### ! Fix
*   **Direct declaration** (shown above) for a single patched artifact in a graph where nothing else requests it.
*   **Add `strictly`** when a transitive might ask for a newer public release:
    ```groovy
    implementation('org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter') {
        version { strictly '2.5.14.ACME' }
    }
    ```
*   **Move to a vendor BOM** once more than a handful of artifacts need patching ([GS16](../scenario-16-private-bom/guide.qmd)).

#### ! Risk
* LOW One patched artifact, declared directly, with a comment naming the CVE or ticket it addresses.
* MEDIUM A patched version that a transitive later out-votes; the build stays green and the patch silently stops being applied.
* HIGH Patched versions sprinkled across many modules with no inventory, so nobody knows which ones are still in force when the vendor ships the next build.

#### ! Control
*   **Filter the private repository** with `content { includeGroup ... }` so only the patched groups are fetched from it.
*   **Verify the patch is applied**, not just declared: `dependencyInsight` shows the selected version and why.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `gradle dependencies --configuration compileClasspath` (run `bash ../../../install_private_repo.sh` once first, or `install_deps.sh`, which calls it)

**What to look for:** `org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter:2.5.14.ACME` with no arrow: the version requested is the version selected.

**Conclusion:** The direct request was satisfied from the private repository, and nothing out-voted it.

#### ! Scales
Direct patches are fine for one or two artifacts and unmanageable beyond that, which is why vendors ship BOMs. The pattern also does not travel: a patched version declared in an application does nothing for the libraries it depends on, whereas a platform applied in a convention plugin reaches every project. Use the direct form for the exception and the BOM for the rule.

#### ! Takeaway
A direct declaration requests a version; it does not guarantee one. For a one-off patch that nothing else contests it is enough, and `strictly` is the word to add when that stops being true.

#### ! Wild

The one-off patch is how most teams first meet a private repository: a CVE lands in a library whose maintainers have moved on, someone builds a fixed jar, publishes it to the company's artifact server with a suffixed version, and declares it in the affected application. It works, and six months later a framework upgrade brings a transitive request for the newer public release, which wins conflict resolution and quietly drops the patch. The teams that notice are the ones that pinned with `strictly` or checked `dependencyInsight` after the upgrade.
